facts.statement: The dinosaur Siats was first described by paleontologists Lindsay E. Zanno and Peter J. Makovicky in 2013.
facts.quote: Siats was described by Lindsay E. Zanno and Peter J. Makovicky in 2013.

facts.statement: The genus name Siats refers to a man-eating monster from Ute mythology.
facts.quote: The generic name references a man-eating monster in Ute mythology.

facts.statement: The species name meekerorum honors geologist John Caldwell Meeker and his family for supporting paleontological research.
facts.quote: The specific name meekerorum honors the geologist John Caldwell Meeker and his family for their support of paleontological research.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Siats was discovered by Lindsay Zanno during a 2008 Field Museum expedition led with Peter Makovicky.
facts.quote: The specimen was discovered by Lindsay Zanno as a part of a 2008 Field Museum expedition with Peter Makovicky.

facts.statement: Siats fossils were collected from the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in Utah, dating to the early Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous about 94.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: It was collected between 2008 and 2010 from the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in Emery County of Utah, dating to the early Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 94.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Siats is known from a single partial postcranial skeleton, specimen FMNH PR 2716, which is housed at the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago.
facts.quote: Siats is known from the holotype specimen, FMNH PR 2716, a partial postcranial skeleton housed at the Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago.

facts.statement: The Siats holotype represents a single individual that was skeletally immature at the time of death, indicated by unfused neural arches.
facts.quote: The Siats holotype specimen consists of material from a single individual that is considered skeletally immature based on the incomplete fusion of neural arches to the centra of the dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Siats is defined by seven unique anatomical traits, four of which are autapomorphies specific to the genus.
facts.quote: Siats is characterized by seven traits, including four autapomorphies.

facts.statement: Distinctive features of Siats include subtriangular distal tail vertebrae, elongated laminae on proximal tail vertebrae, a concaved acetabular rim, and a notch on the lateral brevis shelf.
facts.quote: These include the subtriangular cross section of the distal caudal vertebrae, elongated centrodiapophyseal laminae lacking noticeable infradiapophyseal fossae on the proximal caudals, a transversely concaved acetabular rim of iliac pubic peduncle, and the presence of a notch on the end of the truncated lateral brevis shelf.

facts.statement: Siats possessed broad neural spines on its dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Other notable traits include the broad neural spines on the dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Siats is considered one of the largest known theropod dinosaurs from the mid-Cretaceous period in North America.
facts.quote: Siats represents one of the largest known theropods from the 'mid'-Cretaceous of North America.

facts.statement: Researchers estimated Siats to be approximately 10 meters long and weigh about 3.9 metric tons based on femur circumference regression.
facts.quote: Using a femur circumference regression, Zanno and Mackovicky (2013) estimated its size at around 10 m long and mass at roughly 3.9 MT.

facts.statement: Despite being skeletally immature, the Siats holotype was estimated to be as large as the adult Allosaurus anax and Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: They further wrote that the holotype was already comparable in size to Allosaurus anax and Acrocanthosaurus despite its immaturity.

facts.statement: The genus Siats contains only one known species, Siats meekerorum.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Siats meekerorum.

facts.statement: Siats was initially classified as a megaraptoran, a group of large theropods with debated evolutionary relationships.
facts.quote: It was initially classified as a megaraptoran, a clade of large theropods with controversial relationships.

facts.statement: Scientists have proposed alternative classifications for Siats within the groups Neovenatoridae, Allosauroidea, and Tyrannosauroidea.
facts.quote: Alternative positions within the Neovenatoridae, Allosauroidea, and Tyrannosauroidea have also been proposed.

facts.statement: A 2014 study contested Siats' placement in Megaraptora, suggesting megaraptorans were likely tyrannosauroids rather than neovenatorids like Siats.
facts.quote: In the 2014 description of a juvenile Megaraptor specimen, the referral of Siats to Megaraptora was contested, and megaraptorans were found to more likely be tyrannosauroids rather than neovenatorids such as Siats.

facts.statement: Bell et al. (2016) found Siats' phylogenetic position uncertain, with analyses placing it variously as a relative of ornithomimosaurs, a basal megaraptoran, or a tyrannosauroid closer to tyrannosaurids than Xiongguanlong.
facts.quote: However, Bell et al. (2016) recovered Siats as a member of Coelurosauria of uncertain phylogenetic placement within this group; their analyses found variable positions for Siats, as a relative of ornithomimosaurs, a theropod more closely related to maniraptorans than tyrannosauroids, a basal megaraptoran, or a tyrannosauroid more closely related to tyrannosaurids than Xiongguanlong.

facts.statement: Naish and Cau (2022) recovered Siats as the most basal megaraptoran and suggested it and Chilantaisaurus represented a wave of gigantism in tyrannosauroids before the Tyrannosauridae evolved.
facts.quote: Naish and Cau (2022) recovered the taxon as the basalmost megaraptoran, with this clade diverging after Xiongguanlong, and supported Siats and Chilantaisaurus as representing a wave of gigantism in tyrannosauroids preceding the Tyrannosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2025 analysis by Kellermann, Cuesta, and Rauhut consistently placed Siats within Megaraptora based on shared pneumatic fossa positions.
facts.quote: In their 2025 analysis of allosauroid phylogenetics, Kellermann, Cuesta & Rauhut consistently recovered Siats as a megaraptoran, noting that it shares a specific position of pneumatic fossa with this clade.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Siats spans the Cenomanian stage, from approximately 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Cenomanian (100.5 to 93.9 million years ago)
